notes.h: Scale and pace of urban growth
notes.b: Cities in the developing world (poorer countries, mostly in Asia, Africa and Latin America) now account for most of the world's urban growth. The UN figures below show how big the shift is.
points: Most of the world's urban growth now takes place in developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America, so the fastest-growing cities are no longer in Europe or North America.
About 30% of the world's population was urban (living in towns and cities) in 1950 and about 55% in 2018 (UN, World Urbanization Prospects 2018).
Over half of the world's population has been urban since about 2007, so the world passed the point where city dwellers outnumber rural dwellers.
The UN projects that about 68% of the world's population will be urban by 2050.
Close to 90% of the increase to 2050 is expected in Asia and Africa; India, China and Nigeria together account for over a third of it.
Megacities, with over 10 million people, are a growing feature of urbanisation in the developing world.
UN-Habitat (the UN agency for human settlements) estimates that over 1 billion people live in slums or informal settlements, meaning crowded housing built without legal permission or services.
notes.tip: A general answer on developing-world cities should open with scale: name the regions, then use the UN shares of 30% (1950), 55% (2018) and about 68% (2050).

notes.b: Cities grow in two ways: more babies than deaths, and more people arriving than leaving. In developing countries both are strong at once. There is more on migration theory in the Rural-to-urban migration in developed and developing regions note.
points: Natural increase (births minus deaths): the urban population is young, birth rates are high and death rates have fallen, so the city grows even without newcomers.

Push factors (things that drive people out of the countryside): rural poverty, landlessness, small farms, mechanisation (machines replacing farm workers), drought and crop failure, lack of services, conflict and natural disasters.
Pull factors (things that draw people to the city): jobs in the formal and informal sectors, higher wages, schools and hospitals, perceived opportunities, and family already living in the city.
Primate cities (a country's largest city, far bigger than any other) attract investment and government spending, which reinforces their pull on migrants.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask for reasons or factors behind a city's growth, so give natural increase and then push and pull factors, each with a short explanation.

notes.b: Migrants arrive faster than the city can build homes, and most have little money. They build their own shelter wherever they can, which creates the first and most visible problem of rapid growth.
points: Migrants with little money and no legal land settle in shanty towns, slums and informal settlements, called bustees, favelas, chawls or jhopadpattis depending on the country.
These settlements are built on marginal land (land nobody else wants because it is unsafe or unsuitable): river banks, steep slopes, beside railways, rubbish dumps and floodplains.
Tenure (the legal right to occupy land) is insecure, so residents can be evicted and have no legal right to the land they occupy.
Overcrowding is severe, and some people have no shelter at all, living as homeless pavement dwellers.
notes.tip: Housing problems can be used in a short answer on two problems of rapid urban growth. Give the cause (migrants with no money or legal land) as well as the effect.

notes.b: Informal settlements are built without services, and this directly harms health. Sanitation means the safe disposal of human waste and dirty water.
points: Without piped water or sewers, settlements rely on open drains and shared toilets, so waste stays close to where people live and cook.
Contaminated water and waste spread water-borne disease (illness carried in dirty water): cholera, typhoid and dysentery.
notes.tip: Link cause and effect here: no piped water or sewers leads to open drains, which leads to cholera, typhoid and dysentery.

notes.b: There are not enough regular jobs for all the migrants, so many make a living outside the formal economy. The informal sector means work that is unregistered, untaxed and unprotected.
points: Many residents work in the informal sector as street vendors, rickshaw pullers, waste pickers and home workers.
Informal work offers no job security and low pay; child labour is part of informal employment.
Underemployment means that people have work but not enough of it to earn a living, so they are counted as working yet remain poor.
notes.tip: Name the informal jobs and say what is wrong with them: no security, low pay and child labour.

notes.b: Road and rail systems were built for much smaller populations. When the city expands faster than its transport, movement slows for everyone.
points: Road networks cannot cope with the growth in traffic, so journeys take longer and congestion (traffic jams) becomes permanent.
Trains and buses are overcrowded at peak times, when most people travel to and from work.
Road deaths are a serious problem in the city, because crowded roads mix heavy traffic with pedestrians.

notes.b: Crowded cities with weak services release waste into the air, rivers and streets faster than it can be removed.
points: Air pollution comes from traffic, industry and cooking fuels burned in crowded homes.
Untreated sewage and industrial waste are discharged into rivers, because there are no treatment plants to clean them first.
Rubbish is not collected in many areas, so it builds up in streets and drains.
notes.tip: A pollution answer should separate air, water and rubbish, with a cause for each.

notes.b: Poor people settle on the land most exposed to danger, so natural hazards hit informal settlements hardest.
points: Monsoon (seasonal heavy rain) or tropical downpours flood low-lying, paved and badly drained land, where settlements are often built; paving stops rain soaking into the ground and poor drains cannot carry it away.
Hillside slums are at risk of landslides, and crowded, poorly built homes are at risk of fire.

notes.b: Rapid growth also produces social strains, which weak city government is too stretched to manage.
points: Crime and drugs are social problems, and street children live and work on the streets.
Rich and poor districts sit side by side, so inequality is visible within the city.
Local government is weak, so it struggles to provide services.
notes.tip: For a short answer on two problems, choose from housing, water and sanitation, employment, transport, pollution, flooding and social problems, and explain each with a cause and an effect.

notes.b: The first response to slums is often to remove them. This is the least successful of the solutions.
points: Slum clearance removes informal settlements by demolition and eviction (forcing residents out).
It usually fails, because residents are moved further out or into new slums and the underlying problems (poverty and lack of housing) remain.
notes.tip: If asked to evaluate slum clearance, say it usually fails and give the reason: people end up further out or in new slums.

notes.b: Instead of building homes for people, the authorities prepare land and let residents do the building. No named scheme is needed for this general solution.
points: In a site-and-service scheme the authorities provide serviced plots with water, drains and power.
Residents build their own homes on these plots, which is known as aided self-help (the authorities help with the services, the residents do the building).

notes.b: Upgrading improves a slum where it stands rather than removing it, so nobody has to move.
points: Lanes are paved, water taps, toilets, drains and electricity are installed, and residents are given secure tenure (a legal right to stay).
Because the community stays in place, people can improve their own homes over time, as they no longer fear eviction.

notes.b: Another approach is to build new towns beside the city so that growth goes there instead of into the crowded centre.
points: Planned satellite towns and new towns (towns built beside a large city, with planned housing, jobs and services) divert growth away from the overcrowded core.
Examples are given in the Mumbai case study (Navi Mumbai) and the Kolkata case study (Salt Lake and New Town).

notes.b: Cities cannot solve congestion just by building more roads, so they invest in public transport that carries many people at once.
points: Metros (underground or elevated urban railways), suburban rail and bus rapid transit (buses with their own lanes and fast boarding, working like a train system) move large numbers of people without adding more cars to the roads.
Curitiba in Brazil is the leading example of bus rapid transit, described below.

notes.h: Solution example: Curitiba, Brazil (bus rapid transit)
notes.b: Curitiba, in southern Brazil, shows how a cheap, well-planned bus system can ease traffic in a developing-world city.
points: Bus rapid transit began in Curitiba in 1974 under architect-mayor Jaime Lerner.
Dedicated bus lanes and raised tube stations allow fast boarding, which reduces car use because the bus is quicker than sitting in traffic.
Recyclable waste could be exchanged for food or bus tokens, which tackled rubbish and helped poorer residents at the same time.
The model has been copied worldwide, for example in Bogotá's TransMilenio (2000).
notes.tip: If asked for one solution, Curitiba gives you a named place, a date (1974), a person (Jaime Lerner) and a result (reduced car use).

notes.b: Some solutions act on the push factors in the countryside, so fewer people leave for the city in the first place.
points: Rural development, land reform (giving landless farmers land) and jobs in smaller cities give people reasons to stay in rural areas.
NGOs (non-governmental organisations, i.e. charities) and community groups also act on these problems, as the Missionaries of Charity do in Kolkata.

notes.b: Kolkata (called Calcutta until 2001) is the main developing-world case study. Its site and history explain why it became one of India's largest cities.
points: Kolkata lies on the Hooghly river near the Bay of Bengal, on low-lying delta land (flat land built up by river deposits), which is why it floods easily.
It was founded in 1690 by the British East India Company (Job Charnock).
It developed as a port on the Hooghly, with jute mills (factories making cloth and sacks from the jute plant); Howrah Bridge across the river opened in 1943.
It was the capital of British India until 1911, so government jobs and trade drew people to it.
The city was renamed from Calcutta to Kolkata in 2001.
notes.tip: Kolkata was the capital of British India until 1911. Use the name Kolkata, giving Calcutta once.

notes.b: Kolkata grew because colonial rule built an economy that drew people in, and because disasters and wars then pushed more people towards it.
points: It was a colonial port and administrative capital, and its jute and engineering industries attracted migrants from Bihar, Odisha and rural Bengal.
The Bengal famine of 1943 drove millions of rural people towards the city.
Partition in 1947 (the division of British India into India and Pakistan) brought refugees, and the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War brought a further wave.
Natural increase adds to the population, and the city has regional primacy in eastern India, meaning it dominates the region's economy and services.
Census 2011 gave an urban agglomeration (the built-up city and its suburbs) of about 14.1 million people.
notes.tip: For three factors influencing growth, pick from the port and capital role, the jute industry, the 1943 famine, Partition refugees, the 1971 war, natural increase and regional primacy. Use Census 2011 only for Indian figures.

notes.b: Migrants arriving faster than housing could be built ended up in slums or on the streets.
points: Bustees (slums) house many of the city's poorest people, in overcrowded conditions, because they cannot afford other housing.
Pavement dwellers have no shelter and live on the streets.
Census 2011 counted about 65 million people in slums across India; this is an India-wide figure, not a Kolkata figure.
notes.tip: Do not give a Kolkata slum percentage. The 65 million figure is for the whole of India.

notes.b: Kolkata's economy weakened just as migrants kept arriving, so there were too few jobs.
points: Partition cut the city off from the jute-growing lands that became East Pakistan, so the economy declined because the jute mills lost their raw material.
Jobs did not keep pace with migrants, so many people depend on informal work.
Informal work includes hand-pulled rickshaws; Kolkata is one of the few cities in the world where these still operate.

notes.h: Kolkata: water, flooding, pollution and traffic
notes.b: Services and infrastructure (the basic systems a city runs on) were never built for so many people, and the city's low-lying site adds to the problems.
points: Water supply and sewerage (the system of pipes carrying away waste water) are poor, so many residents lack safe water and proper sanitation.
Monsoon rain floods the low-lying streets of the city.
Air pollution and traffic congestion add to the city's environmental problems.

notes.b: Kolkata's planners, governments and charities have tried housing, transport, new towns and environmental solutions. Together these form the solutions part of the case study.
points: The Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority, the city's planning body, was set up in 1970.
From the 1970s its bustee improvement programme provided water taps, toilets, paved lanes and drains.
Kolkata Metro, India's first, opened in 1984, which eases congestion by moving people underground.
Salt Lake City (Bidhannagar) is a planned township built from the 1960s on reclaimed wetland (wetland drained and filled to make building land) east of the city; its Sector V is an IT hub.
New Town (Rajarhat) was planned from the late 1990s, with IT parks (business parks for information technology firms).
The East Kolkata Wetlands were designated a Ramsar wetland of international importance in 2002; their fish ponds and fields use and naturally treat much of the city's sewage.
Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity in the city in 1950 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain one solution, so pick one response, such as bustee improvement, the metro or the new towns, and give its date and what it did.

notes.b: To judge the responses, ask who benefited and what is left unsolved.
points: Bustee upgrading improved conditions for many residents, but slums remain.
The new towns serve the middle classes more than the poor.

notes.b: Mumbai (called Bombay until 1995) is the second Indian case study. Its natural harbour and its role as a trading centre made it a magnet for migrants.
points: Mumbai was originally seven islands, joined together by land reclamation (building up land from the sea), with a deep, sheltered natural harbour.
It was a British East India Company port, and cotton mills were built there from the 19th century.
Mumbai is India's financial capital, not its political capital; it houses the Reserve Bank of India headquarters and the Bombay Stock Exchange, founded in 1875, Asia's oldest.
It is the centre of the Bollywood film industry, which is another source of jobs that attracts migrants.
The city was renamed from Bombay in 1995.
Migrants come from across India, including Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, drawn by industry and jobs.
Census 2011 gave a Greater Mumbai urban agglomeration (the city plus its built-up suburbs) of about 18.4 million people.
notes.tip: Mumbai is India's financial capital, not its political capital. Use Census 2011 for Indian city figures.

notes.b: Mumbai is built on a narrow strip of land, so space is short and housing is expensive. Many people end up in slums.
points: Dharavi is one of Asia's largest slums, in central Mumbai, with many small home-based industries such as recycling, leather and pottery.
Land and housing costs are very high on the narrow peninsula (a strip of land almost surrounded by water), which limits the space available for housing.
notes.tip: Do not give a population for Dharavi.

notes.h: Mumbai: transport, flooding and water problems
notes.b: Dense population puts pressure on transport and services, and heavy monsoon rain can overwhelm the city.
points: The suburban railway carries several million passengers a day, and its trains are overcrowded.
Road congestion adds to the pressure on the transport network.
On 26 July 2005 about 944 mm of rain fell in one day at Santacruz, flooding the city.
Water supply and sanitation cannot keep pace with the dense population.

notes.b: Mumbai's old industrial base collapsed in the 1980s, which changed where people worked.
points: The Great Bombay textile strike of 1982 led to the closure of most cotton mills.
Mill land was later redeveloped, so the city's industrial base changed, for example away from cotton.

notes.h: Mumbai: planned growth at Navi Mumbai
notes.b: Mumbai's planners tried to relieve the crowded island city by building a second city across the water.
points: Navi Mumbai is a planned twin city across the harbour, begun in the 1970s by CIDCO (City and Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra, set up 1970).
It is designed to take population and industry away from the crowded core of Mumbai.

notes.b: Rehabilitation means rehousing slum dwellers in new buildings, with private developers paying for it.
points: The Slum Rehabilitation Authority, set up in 1995, lets developers rehouse slum dwellers free in new blocks and sell the remaining flats, so the developers pay for it from those sales.
The Dharavi Redevelopment Project was awarded to the Adani Group in 2022, as a plan to rebuild the slum, for example with new housing.

notes.b: New rail and road links ease pressure on Mumbai's transport and tie it to Navi Mumbai.
points: Mumbai Metro Line 1 opened in 2014, so some commuters have an alternative to the overcrowded roads and trains.
The Bandra–Worli Sea Link opened in 2009, a road bridge over the sea that shortens journeys across the city.
The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link (Atal Setu), opened in January 2024, is India's longest sea bridge and links Mumbai to Navi Mumbai.

notes.b: Rehousing gave people new homes but has drawbacks.
points: Rehousing flats under the Slum Rehabilitation Authority are criticised for poor design.
Rehousing is also criticised for breaking up Dharavi's home-based industries, which depended on the slum's layout and community for their work.

notes.h: São Paulo, Brazil: site and early history
notes.b: São Paulo is the Latin American case study. It is not Brazil's capital (that is Brasília) and it is not on the coast.
points: São Paulo lies on a plateau inland from the port of Santos, not on the coast.
It was founded on 25 January 1554 by Jesuit missionaries, long before its coffee and industrial growth.
Santos is now Latin America's busiest container port, which is why trade and growth gathered inland at São Paulo.
notes.tip: São Paulo is inland and is not the capital; Santos is its port.

notes.b: Coffee, immigration and industry each brought a new wave of people to São Paulo.
points: Coffee wealth in the 19th century was exported through Santos and carried by the Santos–Jundiaí railway, opened in 1867.
Immigration from Europe, especially Italy, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Japanese immigration began in 1908 with the ship Kasato Maru; the city has the largest Japanese community outside Japan, centred on the Liberdade district.
From the 1950s São Paulo became Brazil's industrial heartland; car plants, including Volkswagen, opened in the ABC region (Santo André, São Bernardo do Campo and São Caetano do Sul).
Migrants from the drought-prone North-East of Brazil, known as nordestinos, moved to the city to work in its industries.
notes.tip: For factors influencing growth, pick any three of coffee, immigration, industry and migration from the North-East, with a reason for each.

notes.b: Be clear whether a figure refers to the city or the wider metropolitan region, because the two are very different.
points: IBGE (the Brazilian statistics agency) Census 2022 gave the city of São Paulo about 11.5 million people and the metropolitan region about 21 million.
São Paulo is the largest city in South America and in the Southern Hemisphere.
Brazil is over 80% urban, so São Paulo's growth is part of a country-wide shift.
notes.tip: Do not mix the city figure (about 11.5 million) with the metropolitan figure (about 21 million).

notes.b: São Paulo's wealth sits right beside poverty, and informal housing (favelas) is the clearest sign of this.
points: Paraisópolis favela borders the wealthy district of Morumbi, so extreme inequality is visible from one street to the next.
Heliópolis is São Paulo's largest favela.
Crime is a problem in the city, including in its favelas, so inequality has social effects as well as housing ones.

notes.h: São Paulo: traffic, pollution and flooding
notes.b: A very large metropolitan region puts heavy pressure on its roads, air and rivers.
points: Traffic congestion is severe across the metropolitan region.
Air pollution from vehicles and industry adds to the city's environmental problems.
The Tietê river flows through the city and floods in heavy summer rain.

notes.b: Unusually, São Paulo's problem was too little water, not too much.
points: The Cantareira reservoir system (a group of reservoirs) is the main source of the city's water.
During the 2014–2015 drought the Cantareira fell to very low levels, and water rationing (limiting how much water people receive) was introduced.

notes.b: The authorities have tried traffic limits, new transport and new housing.
points: Rodízio, from 1997: cars are banned from central São Paulo at rush hours on one weekday, according to the last digit of the number plate, which cuts the number of cars on the road each day.
The São Paulo Metro opened its first line in 1974, so that people can travel without using the congested roads.
The Rodoanel Mário Covas ring road encircles the metropolitan region, so traffic can bypass the centre; its first section opened in 2002.
Projeto Cingapura (1990s) replaced some favela shacks with apartment blocks on the same sites.
Minha Casa, Minha Vida, a national subsidised housing programme (the state pays part of the cost), was launched in 2009.
notes.tip: Pick one response and explain what it was and what it did, using its date.

notes.b: The measures have made a difference, but not enough.
points: Favela upgrading and transport improvements have helped.
Favelas and traffic congestion persist, because growth has outpaced the measures taken.

keyTerms.definition: A city with over 10 million people.
Growth of a population through births exceeding deaths, without migration.
A condition in rural areas, such as poverty or drought, that drives people to leave.
A feature of a city, such as jobs or services, that attracts migrants.
The largest city in a country, which is much bigger than any other and dominates its economy.
Unregulated work with no job security, such as street vending or waste picking.
An Indian term for a slum or informal settlement.
A Brazilian term for a slum or informal settlement built on land occupied without legal title.
A scheme in which the authorities provide serviced plots and residents build their own homes.
Improving an existing settlement in place with services, paving and secure tenure.
The São Paulo scheme banning cars from central streets at rush hours by number-plate digit.

factCards.term: World urbanisation: UN figures for 1950, 2018 and 2050
factCards.definition: About 30% of the world's population was urban in 1950 and about 55% in 2018, projected about 68% by 2050; over half urban since about 2007. Close to 90% of the increase to 2050 is expected in Asia and Africa. Over 1 billion people live in slums (UN-Habitat).

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: reasons for rapid growth
factCards.definition: Natural increase: a young population, high birth rates, falling death rates. Push: rural poverty, landlessness, mechanisation, drought, conflict. Pull: jobs, higher wages, schools, hospitals, family in the city. Primate cities draw investment.

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: housing problems
factCards.definition: Slums on marginal land: river banks, steep slopes, beside railways, rubbish dumps and floodplains; insecure tenure, so residents can be evicted; severe overcrowding; homeless pavement dwellers.

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: health, employment and transport problems
factCards.definition: No piped water or sewers, so open drains spread cholera, typhoid and dysentery; informal work (vendors, rickshaw pullers, waste pickers) with low pay, no security, child labour and underemployment; overcrowded trains and buses; congestion; road deaths.

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: pollution, hazards and social problems
factCards.definition: Air pollution from traffic, industry and cooking fuels; untreated sewage in rivers; uncollected rubbish; floods on low, badly drained land, landslides on hillside slums, fires; crime, drugs, street children, visible inequality, weak local government.

factCards.term: Slum solutions: why clearance fails and what works better
factCards.definition: Clearance by demolition and eviction usually fails, moving people further out or into new slums. Site-and-service schemes and upgrading in place (paving, taps, toilets, drains, power, secure tenure) keep people housed and let them improve their own homes.

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: other solutions with named examples
factCards.definition: Satellite and new towns divert growth (Navi Mumbai; Kolkata's Salt Lake and New Town); metros, suburban rail and bus rapid transit (Curitiba); rural development, land reform and jobs in smaller cities slow migration; NGOs and community groups help.

factCards.term: Curitiba: how its bus rapid transit works and who copied it
factCards.definition: Begun in 1974 under architect-mayor Jaime Lerner with dedicated bus lanes; raised tube stations for fast boarding were added later; the system cut car use and was copied by Bogotá's TransMilenio (2000). Recyclable waste could be exchanged for food or bus tokens.

factCards.term: Kolkata: reasons for growth
factCards.definition: Colonial port and capital; jute and engineering jobs drew migrants from Bihar, Odisha and rural Bengal; the 1943 Bengal famine; refugees after Partition (1947) and the 1971 Bangladesh war; natural increase. About 14.1 million in Census 2011.

factCards.term: Kolkata: problems of rapid growth
factCards.definition: Bustees and pavement dwellers; overcrowding; poor water and sewerage; monsoon flooding of low-lying streets; air pollution and congestion; Partition cut off the jute lands, so jobs lagged and many rely on informal work, including hand-pulled rickshaws.

factCards.definition: Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority, 1970: bustee improvement with taps, toilets, paved lanes and drains; India's first metro, 1984; Salt Lake City (Bidhannagar) from the 1960s, with the Sector V IT hub; New Town (Rajarhat) from the late 1990s.

factCards.definition: East Kolkata Wetlands, a Ramsar site since 2002, naturally treat much of the city's sewage; Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity (1950; Nobel Peace Prize 1979). Upgrading improved conditions, but slums remain and the new towns serve the middle classes.

factCards.definition: Seven islands joined by reclamation, with a deep sheltered harbour; British East India Company port; cotton mills from the 19th century; financial capital (Reserve Bank of India, Bombay Stock Exchange 1875); Bollywood; migrants from Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

factCards.definition: Navi Mumbai twin city, begun in the 1970s by CIDCO; Slum Rehabilitation Authority (1995): developers rehouse slum dwellers free, then sell other flats; Dharavi project awarded to Adani, 2022. Flats criticised for poor design and breaking up home industries.

factCards.definition: Bandra–Worli Sea Link, 2009; Mumbai Metro Line 1, 2014; Mumbai Trans Harbour Link (Atal Setu), January 2024, India's longest sea bridge, linking Mumbai to Navi Mumbai.

factCards.definition: On a plateau inland from its port, Santos; founded by Jesuits on 25 January 1554; 19th-century coffee wealth carried on the Santos–Jundiaí railway (1867); Italian immigration; Japanese immigration from 1908 (Kasato Maru), centred on Liberdade.

factCards.definition: Brazil's industrial heartland from the 1950s, with car plants such as Volkswagen in the ABC region; nordestinos came from the drought-prone North-East. Census 2022: city about 11.5 million, metropolitan region about 21 million; South America's largest city.

factCards.definition: Favelas: Paraisópolis beside wealthy Morumbi, and Heliópolis, the largest; extreme inequality; severe congestion and air pollution; the Tietê floods in summer rain; the 2014–2015 drought drained the Cantareira reservoirs, causing rationing; crime.

factCards.definition: Rodízio from 1997 bans cars at rush hour on one weekday by plate digit; metro from 1974; Rodoanel ring road from 2002; Projeto Cingapura flats on favela sites (1990s); Minha Casa, Minha Vida (2009). These helped, but favelas and congestion persist.

questions.prompt: Discuss the problems that can arise from the growth of cities in the developing world.
questions.model: Housing is the first problem. Rapid migration has produced bustees, which are overcrowded slums, and pavement dwellers who have no shelter, as in Kolkata. Settlements are built on marginal and low-lying land, so housing is insecure. Water and sewerage are poor, so disease spreads and people lack safe water. Monsoon rain floods the low-lying streets of Kolkata, and flooding damages homes that are already poorly built. Air pollution and traffic congestion add to the city's environmental problems. Employment is a problem because jobs did not keep pace with migrants after Partition cut Kolkata off from its jute hinterland, so many people depend on informal work such as hand-pulled rickshaws. Informal work has no job security and low pay. Social problems include crime and inequality between rich and poor districts. The Census 2011 urban agglomeration of about 14.1 million people shows that the problems affect a very large population. Overall, the growth of the city has outpaced the provision of housing, services and jobs.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one developing-world city that is growing rapidly. (ii) Explain the reasons for its growth. (iii) Describe the problems caused. (iv) Explain one solution.
questions.model: (i) São Paulo, Brazil, is growing rapidly and is the largest city in South America. (ii) Its growth began with coffee wealth in the 19th century, exported through the port of Santos and carried by the Santos–Jundiaí railway from 1867. European immigration, and Japanese immigration from 1908, added to the population. From the 1950s the city became Brazil's industrial heartland, and car plants in the ABC region drew migrants. Migrants from the drought-prone North-East came to work in industry, and the city grew to about 11.5 million people in the city of São Paulo by 2022. (iii) Favelas such as Heliópolis, São Paulo's largest, house many poor people, and Paraisópolis lies beside the wealthy district of Morumbi, which shows extreme inequality. Traffic congestion and air pollution are serious. The Tietê river floods in heavy summer rain. The 2014–2015 drought reduced the Cantareira reservoir system to very low levels, and water rationing followed. Crime is a major problem. (iv) The rodízio scheme, introduced in 1997, bans cars from central São Paulo at rush hours on one weekday, according to the last digit of the number plate. Drivers must use other transport on their banned day, and the metro, whose first line opened in 1974, is one alternative. Favela upgrading and the Projeto Cingapura flats, which replaced some shacks with apartment blocks, are further responses. The rodízio has been a response to traffic congestion, but congestion persists.

questions.prompt: Examine the measures taken to solve the problems of one developing-world city.
questions.model: Mumbai has used several measures. Navi Mumbai, a planned twin city across the harbour begun in the 1970s by CIDCO, set up in 1970, was designed to take population and industry away from the crowded core. It is a long-term planned response, so it does not directly improve the slums that already exist. The Slum Rehabilitation Authority, set up in 1995, lets developers rehouse slum dwellers free in new blocks and sell the remaining flats. This tackles housing directly, but rehousing flats are criticised for poor design and for breaking up Dharavi's home-based industries. The Dharavi Redevelopment Project, awarded to the Adani Group in 2022, applies the same approach to Dharavi, one of Asia's largest slums. Transport measures include Mumbai Metro Line 1, opened in 2014, and the Bandra–Worli Sea Link, opened in 2009. The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link (Atal Setu), opened in January 2024, links Mumbai to Navi Mumbai and is India's longest sea bridge. Transport measures address congestion and the overcrowded suburban railway, but they do not directly improve housing for slum dwellers. Overall, the measures tackle different problems, and the housing schemes are the most criticised.
